central_subject.label: Theory of relativity
central_subject.summary: An umbrella scientific framework comprising special relativity and general relativity, transforming the treatment of spacetime, gravitation, astronomy and modern physics.

nodes.label: Theory of relativity
nodes.description: Umbrella framework comprising Einstein's special and general relativity; special relativity addresses spacetime and physical phenomena absent gravity, while general relativity provides a theory of gravitation and its relation to nature.

nodes.label: Special relativity
nodes.description: Theory of spacetime introduced in Einstein's 1905 paper On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies; based on the principle of relativity and invariance of the speed of light in vacuum.

nodes.label: General relativity
nodes.description: Theory of gravitation developed by Einstein from 1907–1915, published in final form in 1916, using curved spacetime and Einstein field equations.

nodes.label: Four-dimensional spacetime
nodes.description: Unified treatment of space and time introduced by relativity.

nodes.label: Principle of relativity
nodes.description: Laws of physics are the same for observers in inertial frames related by relative motion.

nodes.label: Invariant speed of light
nodes.description: Speed of light in vacuum is the same for all observers regardless of relative motion or source motion.

nodes.label: Relativity of simultaneity
nodes.description: Events simultaneous for one observer may not be simultaneous for another observer in relative motion.

nodes.label: Time dilation
nodes.description: Moving clocks are measured to tick more slowly relative to a stationary observer; gravitational time dilation also occurs in deeper gravitational wells.

nodes.label: Length contraction
nodes.description: Objects are measured to be shortened in their direction of motion relative to an observer.

nodes.label: Finite maximum speed
nodes.description: No physical object, message, or field line can travel faster than light in vacuum.

nodes.label: Mass-energy equivalence
nodes.description: Energy and mass are equivalent and transmutable, expressed by E = mc².

nodes.label: Lorentz transformations
nodes.description: Transformations replacing Galilean transformations in special relativity.

nodes.label: Galilean transformations
nodes.description: Classical-mechanical transformations superseded by Lorentz transformations in relativistic kinematics.

nodes.label: Maxwell's equations
nodes.description: Classical electromagnetism equations describing light as a wave with characteristic velocity.

nodes.label: Classical electromagnetism
nodes.description: Physical theory underlying Maxwell's equations and a key context for special relativity.

nodes.label: Newtonian mechanics
nodes.description: Approximately 200-year-old mechanics framework that relativity superseded as the fundamental kinematic/gravitational framework.

nodes.label: Newtonian gravitation
nodes.description: Classical gravitational theory for which general relativity supplies corrections and ultimately a relativistic replacement.

nodes.label: Equivalence principle
nodes.description: Accelerated motion and being at rest in a gravitational field are locally physically equivalent.

nodes.label: Free fall as inertial motion
nodes.description: In general relativity free-fall motion is inertial motion rather than motion caused by a Newtonian gravitational force.

nodes.label: Curved spacetime
nodes.description: Spacetime curvature used by Einstein to resolve the incompatibility between free-fall acceleration and inertial motion.

nodes.label: Riemannian geometry
nodes.description: Geometric framework developed in the nineteenth century and used to formulate general relativity.

nodes.label: Einstein field equations
nodes.description: Equations relating spacetime curvature to mass, energy and momentum, with cosmological-constant term.

nodes.label: Metric tensor
nodes.description: Solutions of Einstein's field equations are metric tensors defining spacetime geometry and inertial motion.

nodes.label: Spacetime topology
nodes.description: Global/topological structure associated with spacetime solutions.

nodes.label: Gravitation
nodes.description: Interaction described geometrically by general relativity.

nodes.label: Gravitational time dilation
nodes.description: Clocks run slower in deeper gravitational wells.

nodes.label: Perihelion/orbital precession
nodes.description: Orbital precession differing from Newtonian gravitational predictions.

nodes.label: Deflection of light
nodes.description: Light rays bend in a gravitational field.

nodes.label: Frame dragging
nodes.description: Rotating masses drag surrounding spacetime.

nodes.label: Expansion of the universe
nodes.description: General relativity accommodates an expanding universe and components capable of accelerating expansion.

nodes.label: Gravitational waves
nodes.description: Propagating gravitational effects predicted within relativistic gravity; included among extraordinary astrophysical phenomena enabled by relativity.

nodes.label: Neutron stars

source_claims.claim: The theory of relativity comprises special relativity and general relativity, published in 1905 and 1915 respectively.
Special relativity applies to physical phenomena in the absence of gravity; general relativity explains gravitation and its relation to forces of nature.
Relativity transformed theoretical physics and astronomy and superseded a roughly 200-year-old Newtonian mechanics framework.
Relativity introduced unified four-dimensional spacetime, relativity of simultaneity, kinematic/gravitational time dilation and length contraction.
Einstein published special relativity in 1905 building on theoretical and empirical results associated with Michelson, Lorentz, Poincaré and others.
Einstein developed general relativity between 1907 and 1915, with final form published in 1916.
The expression 'theory of relativity' was associated with Planck's 1906 terminology and Bucherer's first use of the expression in the discussion section of that paper.
Special relativity was understood and accepted by the physics community by the 1920s.
General relativity initially appeared less experimentally accessible and mathematically difficult, but became central around 1960 as new techniques and astronomical discoveries developed.
Special relativity rests on the principle of relativity and invariant light speed.
Special relativity predicts relativity of simultaneity, time dilation, length contraction, a finite maximum speed, gravitational signal propagation at light speed, and mass-energy equivalence.
General relativity begins with the equivalence principle and interprets free fall as inertial motion.
Einstein and Marcel Grossmann connected general relativity with Riemannian geometry.
Einstein's field equations relate spacetime curvature to mass, energy and momentum.
General relativity predicts gravitational time dilation, orbital precession, light deflection, frame dragging and cosmic expansion.
Einstein described relativity as a principle theory grounded in established empirical facts and regularities, contrasted with constructive theories.
Relativity is falsifiable and makes predictions testable by experiment.
Michelson–Morley produced null ether-drift results in 1881 and 1887; the result alone did not by itself validate special relativity.
Kennedy–Thorndike tested changes in the magnitude of light velocity between inertial frames and obtained a null result.
Ives–Stilwell tested the transverse Doppler effect and observed the Lorentz-factor correction predicted by special relativity.
General relativity was confirmed through classic tests including Mercury's perihelion precession, solar light deflection, gravitational redshift, equivalence-principle tests and frame dragging.
GPS, GLONASS and Galileo require relativistic corrections for precision because satellites move relative to Earth-bound users and experience Earth's gravitational field.
High-precision time measurement, electron microscopes and particle accelerators are cited as practical systems requiring relativistic considerations.
Maxwell's contemporaries regarded light as propagating through a luminiferous aether, motivating ether-drift experiments.
FitzGerald and Lorentz introduced an ad hoc contraction hypothesis in response to null ether-drift observations.
The article identifies quasars, 3-kelvin microwave background radiation, pulsars and black-hole candidates as developments associated with general relativity's later centrality.
The supplied article includes Einstein's 1916 Relativity, the Special and General Theory among references/further reading.
The source includes original and secondary literature on early ether experiments, special-relativity tests, general relativity, GPS, and Einstein's writings.
The article provides Wikimedia-linked original works and learning resources for relativity.
The supplied page was last edited 28 August 2026 according to its page footer.

semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Special relativity concerns spacetime without gravity; general relativity extends the framework to gravitation through curved spacetime and field equations.
Both alter clock rates but arise in different relativistic contexts: relative motion versus gravitational potential/geometry.
The source explicitly frames relativity as beginning from established empirical regularities rather than assumed microscopic mechanisms.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Null ether result vs proof of special relativity
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: The Michelson–Morley result constrained ether models but, according to the source, did not by itself validate special relativity.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Lorentz/FitzGerald contraction vs relativistic length contraction
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: The historical hypotheses and the relativistic effect can look similar mathematically while having different theoretical meanings.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Free fall vs Newtonian gravitational force
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: General relativity changes the conceptual status of free fall by treating it as inertial motion in curved spacetime.
The source distinguishes metric solutions defining geometry from the broader topological structure of spacetime.
Relativity is modeled as a predictive and falsifiable framework whose predictions are separately tested.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Historical acceptance of SR vs GR
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: The source describes markedly different historical trajectories.
This mathematical replacement is a defining structural feature of special relativity.
The source emphasizes that relativity moved from seemingly remote astronomical predictions to routine engineering requirements.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Theory of relativity vs philosophical relativism
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: The source explicitly warns that the scientific concept should not be conflated with philosophical theories called relativism.

misconceptions.correction: The source says the null result constrained ether interpretations but was not by itself sufficient to discount all ether theories or validate special relativity.

misconceptions.misconception: General relativity was immediately as experimentally central as special relativity.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes general relativity as initially difficult to test and becoming central around 1960.
The source explicitly identifies atomic, nuclear and quantum physics, satellite navigation, precision time, electron microscopes and accelerators as applications.

misconceptions.misconception: Relativity simply modifies Newtonian mechanics without replacing its conceptual structure.
misconceptions.correction: The source emphasizes replacement of Galilean transformations by Lorentz transformations and the geometric reformulation of gravitation.

misconceptions.misconception: General relativity treats gravity as an ordinary force in the Newtonian sense.
misconceptions.correction: The source frames gravity geometrically through curved spacetime and field equations.

misconceptions.misconception: The theory cannot be experimentally falsified.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly calls relativity falsifiable and lists experimental tests.

misconceptions.misconception: Relativistic effects are negligible in modern technology.
misconceptions.correction: GPS, satellite timing and several precision instruments require relativistic corrections.
